transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-05-22
Time: 10:30 AM UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Sara Kim (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood CSM), Maya Lopez (Atlas ML), Jonah Reed (Atlas Platform), Priya Nair (Atlas Security), Amit Shah (Atlas SRE)

Summary: quick follow-up from last week's incident where we saw intermittent 5xx/timeouts on prefix-cached routes under burst traffic. Goal was to review logs, discuss mitigations (retries/backoff/circuit-breakers), and agree next steps for a controlled load test and config changes.

[00:00] Sara Kim: hey everybody, thanks for jumping on. we wanted to keep this short, focused on the reliability incident from thursday afternoon. Ravi, you wanna kick off with the high-level observations?

[00:18] Ravi Patel: yeah sure. so quick recap — we saw a spike in 5xx responses and a handful of timeouts between ~15:12 and 15:37 UTC, mostly on the chat/generate endpoint. errors were predominantly 503 and 504, some upstream grpc timeouts. the KV cache hit rate dropped a bit which increased seq compute.

[00:40] Maya Lopez: right, and from our side we saw client-side retries stack up which pushed concurrency higher, so it felt like a feedback loop. also noticed a few malformed requests coming in from the integration job but not a majority.

[01:05] Jonah Reed: just to add, our autoscaler didn't react fast enough to the sudden burst because the signal was short-lived, and we had a couple of pods spike CPU to 95% and then restart — causing some 5xx cascade.

[01:28] Ravi Patel: yep, restarting helped but obviously not ideal. initial hypothesis: two factors — unexpected traffic burst + retry amplification from client SDKs. we also saw a handful of slow KV cache evictions leading to higher end-to-end latencies.

[01:52] Amit Shah: can you quantify "handful"? are we talking single-digit pods or more widespread?

[02:00] Ravi Patel: more like 3-4 pods in the dedicated pool for this customer. not cluster-wide but enough to create tail-latency effects.

[02:18] Maya Lopez: we ran our internal tracing and saw the p99 jump from ~120ms to ~2.4s for a subset of requests. user-facing timeouts were at 10s so some clients retried after hitting client-side 5s, which cascaded.

[02:44] Sara Kim: ok, thanks. let's talk mitigations — short term and medium. short term we recommended immediate client-side changes: exponential backoff with jitter, cap of 2 retries, and a soft increase of request timeouts to avoid aggressive retries. Ravi, you drafted a recommended retry policy?

[03:05] Ravi Patel: yep, sending that after call. proposed config: initial_delay 200ms, multiplier 2.0, max_delay 2s, max_attempts 2, and add a circuit-breaker that opens after 10 errors/min for a given route for 30s. this reduces retry storms and gives autoscaler time to ramp.

[03:30] Priya Nair: from security/compliance standpoint, we need to ensure that enabling more detailed tracing for this incident doesn't expose PHI. Maya, can you anonymize payloads before sharing logs?

[03:45] Maya Lopez: yes, we'll scrub PHI and send aggregated traces. we already redacted user IDs for the exported spans.

[04:00] Jonah Reed: what's the difference between the dedicated pool behavior and hosted API here? are we hitting different autoscale thresholds?

[04:10] Ravi Patel: good question. dedicated pools have configurable instance counts and a cold-start threshold; hosted API can burst more horizontally across nodes but has stricter multi-tenant throttles. in dedicated, a short sharp spike can exhaust local capacity quicker.

[04:32] Liam O'Connor: and please note that Dedicated has options for "burst capacity" which we can enable temporarily; that avoids pod restarts but costs more. Sara can send details.

[04:46] Sara Kim: yep I'll include burst pricing. for the medium term we recommended: 1) enable client retry policy + circuit-breaker, 2) tune autoscaler with faster ramp (scale buffer), 3) increase KV cache size or tune eviction policy, 4) run a staged load test to validate.

[05:10] Amit Shah: about the KV cache — can you share the eviction metrics and what metrics we should watch?

[05:18] Ravi Patel: we'll share a dashboard. key metrics: cache hit rate, avg KV lookup latency, eviction rate, token compute per second, per-pod CPU. a sustained drop in hit rate is an early warning.

[05:36] Maya Lopez: one question — we sometimes see 5xx that map to model oom vs transport errors; can we differentiate in the logs?

[05:44] Ravi Patel: yes, logs indicate model OOMs are usually immediate out-of-memory messages and accompanied by kernel-level OOM kills; transport 504s show long tail latencies then TLS/grpc timeouts. we'll tag examples.

[06:05] Sara Kim: great. let's cover the plan for the controlled load test. Atlas will run a traffic generator that mimics your production profile but capped to staging capacity; Redwood will standby to collect traces and enable debug flags for a short window. proposed date?

[06:20] Maya Lopez: aiming for 2026-05-26 afternoon. would like a 2-hour window.

[06:28] Ravi Patel: works for Redwood. we'll also enable a temporary circuit-breaker override so we can see behavior under controlled retry storms.

[06:40] Priya Nair: again, be mindful of logs — we need RBAC and limited access to the debug logs.

[06:46] Liam O'Connor: noted; we'll provision a short-lived role for Atlas SREs and provide a link to a read-only dashboard.

[07:00] Jonah Reed: about alerting — current alerts were noisy during the incident. can we tune thresholds to reduce alert fatigue but keep signal?

[07:08] Ravi Patel: yes, recommend alert rules: p95 latency > 800ms for 5m and error rate > 2% for 3m. also an alert for sudden cache hit rate drop > 10% in 2m.

[07:24] Maya Lopez: sounds good. one outstanding ask from our infra team is whether Redwood can provide a per-request id for tracing that we can correlate in our logs.

[07:32] Sara Kim: we already emit a request_id header; maybe the SDK doesn't propagate it — Ravi will verify SDK propagation and add an example snippet.

[07:46] Ravi Patel: yep I'll send an SDK patch and sample logs. also will include a suggested client-side backoff lib call for the Node and Python SDKs.

[08:00] Amit Shah: curious — did you see any RATELIMIT (429) events interleaved with 5xxs? could be rate-limit backpressure causing retries.

[08:10] Ravi Patel: there were some 429s earlier in the spike window as the ingress throttles kicked in for a minute. so interplay of 429->retry could've amplified the problem. hence the need for capped retries.

[08:30] Maya Lopez: ok, for our action items we'll 1) run the staged load test on 5/26, 2) apply client-side retry changes in a canary to 10% traffic, 3) provide scrubbing for logs, and 4) review autoscaler tuning after the test.

[08:52] Sara Kim: perfect. before we close, Ravi, anything else from the infra side?

[08:58] Ravi Patel: one last note — for dedicated customers we can enable "warm spare" instances so spikes are absorbed; it's more of a capacity-seat decision. also recommend enabling prefix caching where it makes sense to reduce KV lookups.

[09:20] Jonah Reed: we'll review cost vs. risk for warm spares. if we see repeated incidents, likely worth it.

[09:30] Sara Kim: ok let's recap next steps (quick): Redwood to share logs and dashboard links by 5/24; Ravi sends retry/circuit-breaker config and SDK examples by 5/25; Atlas runs load test 5/26 and shares results; follow-up deep-dive 5/28. action items in the notes.

[09:58] Maya Lopez: thanks everyone, appreciate the fast response.

[10:02] Sara Kim: thanks all, talk soon.

End of transcript.
